source: Lavie, Beck, Konstantinou (2014) Blinded by the load: attention, awareness and the role of perceptual load
finding: States the theory in its own words. Perception has limited capacity but runs automatically on everything within capacity. High load uses all capacity, so nothing is left for distractors. Low load leaves spare capacity that spills over to irrelevant items. Top-down settings say what is relevant, but only load prevents spillover.
numbers: No new numbers for the core claim. Load is raised by more heterogeneous items or by more perceptual operations on the same items.
quote: Effective selective and focused attention therefore requires not just active maintenance of a top-down attentional priority
limits: Theory is about perception, not memory or reasoning. Load must be perceptual; other load types act differently.
agent_relevance: Selection by instruction alone (tell the model to ignore X) is not enough. Spillover is a property of spare capacity, so an easy task leaves room for intrusion (S1).

source: Lavie, Beck, Konstantinou (2014) section 2: distractor measures
finding: Perceptual load reduces response competition from incompatible distractors, even at fixation, and reduces negative priming and capture by irrelevant salient items. Load of a different kind (working memory) gives the opposite effect: more distractor interference.
numbers: Treisman and Geffen: 87% of attended target words detected vs 8% of unattended. Early/late selection debate unresolved for decades before load theory.
limits: RT effects can come from unconscious priming or from de-prioritising the response, so they do not prove reduced awareness.
agent_relevance: Two kinds of difficulty have opposite effects: perception-heavy difficulty shields, control-heavy difficulty exposes. Our difficulty grid must separate them.

source: Lavie and Tsal (1994) Perceptual load as a major determinant of the locus of selection in visual attention
finding: Founding paper. Proposes that the locus of selection (early or late) depends on perceptual load of the relevant task. Cited in the sources we opened as the origin of the theory. Not opened this session.
numbers: No numbers verified by us.
limits: Not read; only described by Tan 2015, Benoni and Tsal 2013 and Forster and Lavie 2009.
agent_relevance: Same as the theory line. Cite as origin only.

source: Lavie (1995) Perceptual load as a necessary condition for selective attention
finding: Founding experiment. Response-competition (flanker-style) paradigm: distractor interference present in low-load displays and removed in high-load displays. Described second-hand as the classic result. Not opened.
numbers: Exact RT figures not verified. Forster and Lavie 2008 replication shows the same pattern with M = 36 ms (low) vs -4 ms (high).
limits: Set-size manipulation of load later challenged as a dilution confound (see a19 to a22).
agent_relevance: Core prediction to test in the agent: distractor effect should shrink as the relevant task gets more demanding on perception.

source: Lavie and Cox (1997) On the efficiency of visual selective attention: efficient visual search leads to inefficient distractor rejection
finding: Search task with a distractor; distractor interference falls only when set size is large enough. Described second-hand by Benoni and Tsal 2013. Not opened.
numbers: Per Benoni and Tsal 2013: going from set size one to four raised RT but did not reduce interference; interference fell only from set size six.
quote: as long as the number of items in the relevant display does not exceed capacity, then irrelevant distractors are not rejected from processing
limits: Benoni and Tsal call this circular: load is judged by whether interference falls, not by an independent measure.
agent_relevance: Load is a threshold effect, not a smooth one. Mild increases in difficulty may not protect against intrusion.

source: Forster and Lavie (2008) Failures to ignore entirely irrelevant distractors: the role of load
finding: Replicated the load effect for response-competing distractors. Also showed that a fully irrelevant distractor (a cartoon character) slows search as much as a response-incongruent letter, and that high load removes this too in later experiments.
numbers: Exp 1, N=16, display until response: congruency effect 36 ms at low load (t(15)=4.18, d=2.16), -4 ms at high load; load x congruency F(1,15)=5.19, p=.038. Irrelevant distractor effect in Exp 1 was NOT modulated by load (F<1). Exp 2(a), 100 ms displays: congruency 25 ms low vs -7 ms high; irrelevant distractor 52 ms at low load. Later experiments: irrelevant distractor 60 and 25 ms at low load, 6 ms at high load (t<1).
limits: Exp 1 with long displays gave interference at both loads for the irrelevant item (authors suggest rarity, meaningfulness). Eye movements possible with long displays; later experiments used 100 ms.
agent_relevance: Entirely off-topic content can still cost speed when the task is easy. Strongest human analogue to a stray irrelevant sentence in a prompt.

source: Forster and Lavie (2009) Harnessing the wandering mind: the role of perceptual load
finding: Task-unrelated thoughts (mind wandering) also fall under high perceptual load. Individual load effects on thoughts and on response competition were correlated.
numbers: Four experiments. Exp 1a N=10, 1b N=14. RT low vs high load 486 vs 644 ms (1a), 490 vs 706 ms (1b). Errors 7.2% vs 16.4% (1a), 4.7% vs 9.9% (1b). Thought probes reporting a TUT: 61.6% low vs 48.9% high (1a); 57.5% vs 44.0% (1b). Mean TUT rate 52.6%.
limits: Small samples. Self-report probe. Alternative accounts (verbal working memory, motivation, response demands) ruled out by the authors, not by us.
agent_relevance: Internal intrusions (off-task thoughts) follow the same rule as external ones. Suggests a free-running agent with an easy task may drift more.

source: Bahrami, Lavie, Rees (2007) Attentional load modulates responses of human primary visual cortex to invisible stimuli
finding: Load effects do not need awareness. V1 response to invisible, continuously suppressed images was lower under a high-load central task (conjunction monitoring) than a low-load one (pop-out monitoring).
numbers: fMRI, N=7 (t(6)=5.79 for RT difference, p=.001). Localisation of hidden tools at chance in both loads (p=.92 and .74). Mask-only BOLD not affected by load (p>.40 in V1, V2, V3).
limits: Tiny sample. Spillover to invisible items does not make them conscious.
agent_relevance: Intrusion can be sub-threshold: content may influence processing without being used in the answer.

source: Macdonald and Lavie (2008) Load induced blindness
finding: High load lowers sensitivity (d') for detecting an expected peripheral squiggle, not just response bias. Working memory load did not do this (per abstract).
numbers: Exp 1, N=15: search RT 766 ms high vs 593 ms low (F(1,14)=8.68); errors 11% vs 3%; d' lower at high load F(1,14)=15.44, p=.002; criterion beta 5.5 vs 9.0, F<1. Hit rate near/far targets 61% vs 64%.
limits: Only Exp 1 numbers extracted. Detection response made first in some experiments to address forgetting.
agent_relevance: Load changes what is registered, not just what is reported. Self-reports of noticing are weak evidence for what the model processed.

source: Cartwright-Finch and Lavie (2007) The role of perceptual load in inattentional blindness
finding: Cross task and search task with a surprise unexpected stimulus on the last trial. Higher load produced much more inattentional blindness. Described via the Lavie 2014 review; not opened.
numbers: Review says baseline awareness at low load varied across experiments while the load effect stayed similar in size. Exact percentages not verified by us.
limits: Surprise-question measure confounded with rapid forgetting and response criterion (review, section 4a).
agent_relevance: A heavy main task can blind the agent to an unexpected but important input. Relevant to missed side information.

source: Macdonald and Lavie (2011) Visual perceptual load induces inattentional deafness
finding: Visual load makes people miss a clearly audible tone. Capacity is shared across senses.
numbers: Exp 1 (cross task, N=56): aware of tone 21 of 28 at low load vs 7 of 28 at high load, chi2(1)=14.00. Exp 2 (N=48, tone alone): 21 of 24 vs 5 of 24, chi2=21.48. Exp 3 N=64. Inattentional deafness reached 79% at high load. Cross task errors 14% vs 0% (Exp 1), 17% vs 3% (Exp 2).
limits: Single critical trial per person (between subjects). Later work (a29) finds load effects on mismatch negativity weak.
agent_relevance: Load in one channel can suppress another. Heavy code or table input may suppress attention to a text note.

source: Raveh and Lavie (2015) Load-induced inattentional deafness
finding: Four experiments: high visual load reduced auditory detection sensitivity even when the tone was expected (50% present) and when the tone was reported first.
numbers: Exp 1, N=17: search RT 935 ms vs 706 ms (F(1,16)=9.88), errors 19% vs 6% (F(1,16)=12.79); detection lower at high load (d' in table, not read in full).
limits: Detection numbers beyond the search check not extracted.
agent_relevance: Supports shared rather than modality-specific capacity.

source: Lavie, Beck, Konstantinou (2014) novel experiment: perceptual load and the contrast response function
finding: High load shifts the contrast response function to the right (contrast gain), like turning stimulus contrast down, without changing asymptote or slope. Offers a mechanism for load blindness.
numbers: N=14. Visual memory accuracy 95% (low) vs 64% (high), d=1.91. Contrast threshold 18% (SD 8) low vs 27% (SD 13) high, t(13)=2.64, p=.023, d=0.79. Asymptote 80% vs 79% (p=.85). Gabor contrasts 0.1 to 90%, 384 trials.
limits: Small N. Load induced by a memory-encoding task, so it blends perceptual and memory encoding load.
agent_relevance: Load acts like lowering the signal strength of the unattended item: weak distractors vanish first, strong ones may still get through.

source: Lavie, Beck, Konstantinou (2014) section 4: attentional blink and dynamic inattentional blindness
finding: High load also deepens the attentional blink and removes the semantic N400 for the second target. In a motion-tracking task, faster tracking made fewer people notice a crossing cross.
numbers: Dynamic IB: 32% noticed at high load vs 71% at low load. Muggleton et al: TMS phosphene threshold rose under high load.
limits: Reported second-hand inside the review.
agent_relevance: Different task types show the same signature; load is not tied to one paradigm.

source: Lavie, Lin, Zokaei, Thoma (2009) The role of perceptual load in object recognition
finding: Distractor object recognition (repetition priming and surprise memory) drops under high load; at low load distractor recognition does not depend on a change of view.
numbers: Abstract-level result statements only; numbers not extracted.
limits: Numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: Even full recognition of unattended items, not only RT effects, depends on load.

source: Tan et al. (2015) Perceptual load and working memory guidance (PLoS ONE)
finding: A cue held in memory biases attention to a matching distractor at low load but not at high load. ERP: P1 validity effect at both loads, N1 effect only at low load.
numbers: WM group N=18 analysed (22 recruited); priming group N=20. RT load F(1,36)=635.19. WM validity effect at low load F(1,17)=13.87, p<.01; at high load F<1. N1 -9.13 uV high vs -8.44 uV low load, F(1,36)=22.03.
limits: Compares holding a cue vs only identifying it, not a memory load level.
agent_relevance: What the prompt keeps in focus (lessons, examples) pulls attention to matching content, mainly when the task is easy.

source: Gutteling, Sillekens, Lavie, Jensen (2022) Alpha oscillations reflect suppression of distractors with increased perceptual load
finding: MEG: high load raises alpha power contralateral to the distractor (suppression) and raises target excitability (frequency tagging). Behaviour: distractor salience cost only at low target load.
numbers: N=30 (df 1,29). Target load F=132.1, partial eta2=.82. Salience effect F=6.7, p=.015. Load x salience F=12.9, p=.001, partial eta2=.31; no salience effect at high load.
limits: Alpha power is also driven by distractor nature, as the authors admit.
agent_relevance: Gives an active suppression plus target-gain mechanism, not pure capacity exhaustion. A scaffold may need both amplify-target and suppress-distractor steps.

source: Remington, Swettenham, Lavie (2012) Lightening the load: perceptual load impairs visual detection in typical adults but not in autism
finding: Individual-differences test. Adults with autism show a different load profile for detecting a peripheral stimulus. Search set sizes 1, 2, 4, 6.
numbers: 16 ASD vs 16 typical adults. Search RT set size effect F(3,78)=13.899; no group main effect (p=.933) or interaction (p=.264).
limits: Small clinical sample. Detection results taken from title only; not extracted.
agent_relevance: Capacity varies between observers; agent variants (model sizes) may differ in capacity.

source: Benoni and Tsal (2013) Conceptual and methodological concerns in the theory of perceptual load
finding: Critique. (1) Load theory is early selection with variable efficiency, not a hybrid. (2) Load is never independently defined; RT is a poor load check; interference itself sometimes serves as the load check, which is circular. (3) Dilution may explain the set-size effect.
numbers: Lavie and Cox 1997: set size 1 to 4 did not cut interference; set size 6 did. Lavie and Robertson 2001: set size 2 to 3 cut interference by almost 200 ms without raising RT.
quote: the major building block of load theory, perceptual load, is a vague term that has never been clearly and precisely defined
limits: Authors are the leading dilution proponents; critique is partisan but specific.
agent_relevance: If our load levels are defined by the effect we want to see, our test is circular. Define load by an independent metric (tokens, steps, items) before running.

source: Benoni and Tsal (2013) alternatives: salience, similarity, object grouping, attentional set
finding: Other accounts: Eltiti 2005 found salience (onset vs offset) beats load; Paquet and Craig 1997: similarity and distance matter; Chen 2003 and Cosman and Vecera 2012: same-object distractors interfere at high load; Theeuwes 2004: mixing load levels abolishes the load effect (attentional set).
numbers: Eltiti: efficient selection for onset target with offset distractor even at low load, interference for offset target with onset distractor even at high load.
limits: Second-hand summary of other papers.
agent_relevance: Distractor similarity and grouping matter as much as load; vary these in tests.

source: Tsal and Benoni (2010); Wilson et al. (2011) dilution evidence, as summarised by Benoni and Tsal (2013)
finding: Low-load, high-dilution displays (neutral letters present but easy task) removed or sharply reduced distractor interference. With dilution controlled, high load gave MORE interference (reversed load effect).
numbers: Interference eliminated in low-load high-dilution displays (Benoni and Tsal 2010; Tsal and Benoni 2010a); markedly reduced (Wilson et al. 2011).
limits: Chen and Cave 2013 find dilution is itself conditional (a22). Second-hand.
agent_relevance: The set-size effect may come from crowding by neutral items, not exhausted capacity. Surrounding filler text could do the work load was credited with.

source: Chen and Cave (2013) Perceptual load vs. dilution: attentional focus, stimulus category, target predictability
finding: Four experiments. Neutral items reduce distractor processing only when attentional focus is broad, when neutral items share the target category, and when target knowledge is insufficient to guide search. Both accounts alone are too simple.
numbers: Exp 1: RT 655 ms (2 cues) vs 759 ms (6 cues). Congruency effect 78 ms with 6 cues vs 42 ms with 2 cues; 69 ms with 2 letters vs 51 ms with 6 letters (dilution effect).
limits: Dilution effect modest (18 ms).
agent_relevance: Boundary conditions: filler helps only if it looks like the target and the target is hard to find.

source: Scalf, Torralbo, Tapia, Beck (2013) Competition explains limited attention and perceptual resources
finding: Biased-competition view: limited capacity is neural competition among stimuli. Distractor processing depends on competition plus the bias applied. Compatible with parts of both load and dilution.
numbers: Review; no new numbers.
limits: Conceptual; predictions overlap with both rivals.
agent_relevance: A graded mechanism that predicts both load and dilution effects and that a prompt can bias.

source: Neokleous, Shimi, Avraamides (2016) Modeling the effects of perceptual load: saliency, competitive interactions, top-down biases
finding: Computational model of visual selective attention with saliency maps, lateral competition and top-down bias. It reproduces the load pattern, central distractors interfering at high load (Beck and Lavie 2005), cueing removing low-load interference, and a dilution result. It uses no definition of load.
numbers: Simulations match the pattern; magnitudes differ from human data in some sets. No fit statistics read.
limits: Qualitative match only. One of few formal models of the theory.
agent_relevance: Load effects can emerge from competition plus bias with no explicit load variable; a template for a code-checked distractor model.

source: Snowden et al. (2025) Reduction in distraction due to perceptual load: a failure to replicate
finding: Six experiments found no reduction of distraction or congruence effects with high load, with central or peripheral distractors, long or 200 ms displays, more or less load. Also contradicts dilution.
numbers: Exp 1 N=36 (3 removed): distraction 56 ms low vs 67 ms high (d=0.80 vs 0.60, no difference), congruence 197 ms vs 202 ms; load x distractor F(1.8,63.7)=0.05, p=.98. Exp 2 N=32 (200 ms): distraction 58.5 vs 42.4 ms; congruence 207.5 vs 160.8 ms; interaction p=.05. Exp 5 N=19. Exp 6 N=34.
quote: Our findings thus do not support the tenants of perceptual load theory
limits: Single lab. Load levels small (high load = 4 elements). Peripheral distractor effects weaker. Measure was inverse-efficiency score.
agent_relevance: Most important caution: the effect may not be general. Do not assume a monotone load shield; test it in the agent.

source: Snowden et al. (2025) discussion of boundary conditions (Theeuwes 2004, Roper and Vecera 2013, Eayrs 2024, Cosman and Vecera 2012)
finding: Load effects depend on design: interleaved vs blocked load, display duration (mnemonic load), object grouping, and previous-trial load. Distraction appears at high load when load is mixed trial by trial.
numbers: Roper and Vecera 2013: classic result at brief displays; congruence at high load with long displays. Theeuwes 2004: distraction at both loads when interleaved, not when blocked. Eayrs 2024: reduced distraction only when high load was cued and the previous trial was also high.
limits: Second-hand description.
agent_relevance: Whether the shield works may depend on a stable mode set by earlier steps. Rapid switching of task difficulty may remove it.

source: de Fockert (2013) Beyond perceptual load and dilution: working memory in selective attention (meta-analysis)
finding: Working-memory load increases distractor processing; high working-memory capacity lowers it. This is the load-theory prediction for cognitive-control load, opposite to perceptual load.
numbers: 26 studies (49 experiments): mean r = 0.202, t(48)=2.95, p<.005. 35 experiments showed more distraction vs 14 less (chi2=9.0, p<.01). Capacity: 12 studies mean r = 0.286, t(11)=7.92.
limits: Publication bias acknowledged. Small, mixed paradigms.
agent_relevance: Two opposite difficulty effects: perceptual load protects, control load (holding many items) exposes. Long reasoning chains that tax working memory may raise intrusion.

source: Hung, Wu, Shimojo (2020) Task-induced attention load guides and gates unconscious semantic interference (Nat Commun)
finding: Unconscious word processing is gated by task load: a subliminal prime slowed responses when the task was naming the word (low load) but not when naming its colour (high load), unless practice made the colour task easy.
numbers: n=20 per experiment. Late trials in colour naming: word-incongruent trials 5.36% slower vs 0.62% for congruent. Replicated in word-only and semantics-only experiments.
limits: Small n per experiment.
agent_relevance: Semantic, not only visual, intrusion is gated by load; practice (lower load) lets distractors back in.

source: Wiens, Szychowska, Nilsson (2016) Visual task demands and auditory mismatch negativity: empirical study and meta-analysis
finding: A new study (N=28) found no load reduction of the auditory mismatch negativity; the pooled analysis still supports a reduction but is small and fragile.
numbers: Pooled k=6, N=97: mean difference -0.46 uV [-0.72, -0.20]; I2=20%. With k=7, N=106: dz=-0.34; power of included studies .15 to .41. Authors urge preregistered n>150.
limits: Small, underpowered, possible winner's curse.
agent_relevance: Neural load effects may be inflated in the literature. Weigh small studies lightly.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context (GSM-IC)
finding: Adding one irrelevant sentence to grade-school math problems sharply lowers accuracy. Fewer than 30% of base problems stay solved across all distractor variants. Self-consistency, exemplars with distractors and an ignore-instruction help.
numbers: Table 3 (code-davinci-002, plain exemplars): COT micro 72.4%, macro 6.0%; LTM micro 77.5%, macro 18%; PROGRAM micro 54.4%. With instruction: COT 77.8%, LTM 80.6%. Self-consistency (20 samples): COT 88.1% micro, LTM 93.4% micro; best macro 45%. text-davinci-003: COT 68.4 micro / 9.0 macro; LTM 71.3 / 12.0. Drop largest for COT and PROGRAM at 4+ steps.
quote: Solve grade school math problems. Feel free to ignore irrelevant information given in the questions.
limits: Old models (2022 to 2023). Not framed as load theory. Role overlap and number-in-range of the distractor matter most.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that an irrelevant sentence harms LLMs. Harm grows with more reasoning steps for COT, the opposite of a high-load shield. An ignore instruction added 4 to 5 points.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Lost in the middle: how language models use long contexts
finding: Multi-document QA accuracy is U-shaped by position: best at start or end of context, worst in the middle. In worst cases accuracy falls below closed-book.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo: closed-book 56.1%, oracle 88.3%. Tested with 10, 20, 30 documents. Drop of over 20% in the worst position; at 20 and 30 documents the middle position fell below closed-book.
limits: Distractor documents are retrieved passages, not unrelated filler. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: More distractors can reduce use of the relevant item, the reverse of a high-load shield. Keep key content at start or end.

source: Yoran et al. (2023) Making retrieval-augmented language models robust to irrelevant context
finding: Irrelevant retrieved text can hurt: even top-1 search results lowered accuracy on StrategyQA and Fermi; random contexts dropped accuracy sharply on all five datasets. Fine-tuning on 1,000 mixed examples gave robustness.
numbers: Five datasets; 1,000 examples suffice (as stated). Per-dataset accuracies not extracted.
limits: Needs fine-tuning, which our scaffold does not use. Numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Scaffold-level fix is to filter irrelevant retrieved content in code (G5), not to ask the model to ignore it.

source: Levy, Jacoby, Goldberg (2024) Same task, more tokens: impact of input length on reasoning (FLenQA)
finding: Padding a fixed reasoning task with irrelevant text lowers accuracy at lengths far below the maximum context. Next-word loss correlates negatively with reasoning performance.
numbers: Headline case: accuracy fell from 0.92 to 0.68 with added tokens. Several models, padding types and locations; chain-of-thought did not remove the drop.
limits: Padding is irrelevant filler of several kinds; not the same as dilution by similar items.
agent_relevance: Filler around the task hurts LLMs, against the human dilution effect. Keep the working prompt short.

source: Gap note: no LLM test of perceptual load theory found in sources opened
finding: None of the papers opened tests Lavie's theory directly in an LLM with a load by distractor grid. LLM work found (a30 to a33) tests irrelevant context, position and length only. The web search quota was used up, so a wider 2020-2026 LLM search was not possible here.
numbers: None.
limits: The gap may be due to search limits, not to absence of papers.
agent_relevance: Our own distractor-by-difficulty grid (SUBFIELDS question 1) is likely new; plan to run it.
